deep.reconstruction:
This is the manuscript of §13 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854; published by Dedekind in 1867). The previous page is the end of §5 on the integral concept.

(A) Claim. A function can be integrable throughout, in the extended (improper) sense, without being representable by its Fourier series. The published text reads 'welche unendlich viele Maxima und Minima hat'; see the corrections below.

Example: on (0,2π), f(x) = d/dx[x^ν cos(1/x)] with 0<ν<1/2. Explicitly f = ν x^(ν-1) cos(1/x) + x^(ν-2) sin(1/x). This f is unbounded near 0. Its integral up to 0 still exists as an improper integral, because x^ν cos(1/x) → 0.

The Fourier integral ∫_0^{2π} f(x) cos n(x−a) dx gets an ever-growing contribution from x ≈ 1/√n. Its ratio to ½ √π sin(2√n − na + π/4) n^{(1−2ν)/4} tends to 1. Since (1−2ν)/4 > 0, the Fourier coefficients are unbounded and the series cannot converge.

(B) General setting. Let ∫f dx = φ(x) cos ψ(x), with φ → 0 and ψ → ∞ as x → 0+. Away from 0, φ and ψ are smooth with finitely many extrema. Then:
- f = φ' cos ψ − φ ψ' sin ψ.
- By product-to-sum, ∫ f cos n(x−a) dx equals the sum of four integrals: ½∫φ' cos(ψ ± n(x−a)) dx and −½∫φψ' sin(ψ ± n(x−a)) dx.

Take the term −½∫ φ ψ' sin(ψ + n(x−a)) dx, with ψ positive and hence ψ' < 0. Put y = ψ(x) + n(x−a). The sign changes of sin y are slowest where dy/dx = 0, i.e. ψ'(α) = −n. This is a stationary point.

Now localize to [α−ε, α+ε], with ε → 0 as n → ∞. Let β = ψ(α) + n(α−a).
- Taylor: y = β + ψ''(α)(x−α)²/2 + …, with ψ''(α) > 0 because ψ' increases from −∞.
- Hence dy/dx = ψ''(α)(x−α) = ±√(2ψ''(α)(y−β)), the sign following that of x−α.
- Freeze φψ' at α and substitute y as the variable. Both halves of the interval give the same integral, so
  −½∫_{α−ε}^{α+ε} φψ' sin y dx = ½(∫_{β+δ}^{β} − ∫_β^{β+δ}) sin y dy/√(y−β) · φ(α)ψ'(α)/√(2ψ''(α)), where δ = ψ''(α)ε²/2.
- This equals −∫_0^{δ} sin(y+β) dy/√y · φ(α)ψ'(α)/√(2ψ''(α)).

Continued on the next page: let δ → ∞ and use the Fresnel value ∫_0^∞ sin(y+β) y^(−1/2) dy = √π sin(β+π/4).

My check of the example: ψ = 1/x gives α = n^(−1/2), β = 2√n − na, φ(α) = n^(−ν/2), ψ'(α) = −n and ψ''(α) = 2n^(3/2). Then −sin(β+π/4) √(π/(2ψ'')) φψ' = ½√π sin(2√n − na + π/4) n^{(1−2ν)/4}. This confirms the stated asymptotic.
errors: The change of variables freezes φψ' at x=α and drops the higher Taylor terms of y. This is justified only for a suitable choice of ε, a point Riemann leaves implicit. For ψ=1/x one needs n^(3/2)ε² → ∞ (so that δ → ∞) together with n²ε³ → 0 and ε/α → 0, e.g. n^(−3/4) ≪ ε ≪ n^(−2/3). Such a window exists, so the result stands, but the step is only heuristic on this page.

Also left unproven: that the other three integrals, and the parts of the stationary-phase integral away from α, contribute o(main term). These are asserted on the next page ('übrige Bestandtheile unendlich klein').

The intermediate line with ½(∫_{β+δ}^{β} − ∫_β^{β+δ}) carries the dx = ±dy/√(2ψ''(y−β)) sign implicitly; written with dy/√(y−β) alone it is consistent only once that sign is understood. The final result −∫_0^δ sin(y+β) dy/√y · φψ'/√(2ψ'') is correct.

The phrase 'welche nicht unendlich viele Maxima und Minima hat' (if that is the reading) contradicts the example. f = d(x^ν cos(1/x))/dx has infinitely many extrema near 0. The published text says 'welche unendlich viele Maxima und Minima hat'. So either the transcription is wrong or the manuscript has a slip.

results.what: An improperly integrable function on [0,2π] (unbounded, infinitely oscillating) whose Fourier coefficients do not tend to zero, indeed grow like n^{(1−2ν)/4}. Example: f = d(x^ν cos(1/x))/dx, 0<ν<1/2. So integrability does not imply Fourier representability.
results.modern_name: Failure of the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma for improper (non-absolutely convergent) Riemann integrals; counterexample to Fourier representability

results.what: Asymptotic evaluation of an oscillatory integral by localizing at the point where the phase is stationary (ψ'(α)+n=0), using a quadratic phase and the Fresnel integral.
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes (1856) and Kelvin (1887); Riemann's 1854/1867 use (and his saddle-point work of 1863) is a recognized early instance

results.what: Product-to-sum decomposition of ∫ f cos n(x−a) into four integrals.

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the manuscript of §13 of Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift. The counterexample and the stationary-phase argument are well known and attributed to him. The only interest is manuscript-level variants (e.g. the 'nicht' reading and the phase constant inserted into the asymptotic).

transcription_corrections: Line 3: 'eine Function f(x) welche nicht unendlich viele Maxima und Minima hat' should probably read 'welche unendlich viele Maxima und Minima hat', as in the published text and as the example requires. If the manuscript really has 'nicht', it is a slip.

The asymptotic comparison quantity should read ½ sin(2√n − na + π/4) √π n^{(1−2ν)/4}. The '+π/4' (written as an insertion above the line) belongs inside the sine argument. My computation confirms +π/4.
'wo x nahe = √(1/n) ist' is correct; the stationary point is at x = n^(−1/2).

'ψ(x) positiv genommen' is plausible: ψ → +∞. The insertion near 'und zwar ist' should read roughly 'und zwar ist ψ''(α) positiv, da ψ(x) für ein unendlich kleines x positiv unendlich wird'. The struck-out text there was not 'ψ'(x)' as transcribed.
In the line '... (den Grenzwerth des Ausdrucks)' the struck word is 'Integral', replaced by 'Verhalten des Integrals'; the transcription is correct.
